whyFailCards.desc: PAL multipliers (sedentary, lightly active, very active) are rough categories. The difference between 'lightly active' and 'moderately active' can be 200–400 kcal/day. Almost no one knows exactly which they belong to.

whyFailCards.title: Adaptive thermogenesis is ignored
whyFailCards.desc: During a longer cut your actual TDEE drops by 150–300 kcal compared to the formula — the body reduces NEAT and BMR in response to energy deficit. A static calculator never accounts for this.

whyFailCards.title: The formula doesn't fit all body types
whyFailCards.desc: Mifflin-St Jeor is the most validated formula but has a confidence interval of ±10%. For someone with a TDEE of 2500 kcal that means a possible error of ±250 kcal — enough to derail a cut.

best-tdee-calculator.whyFailOutro: The solution is not a better formula — it's a system that measures your actual weight trend and calibrates the TDEE estimate against reality. That's exactly what Calculeat does.

faq.question: Which TDEE calculator is most accurate?
faq.answer: No static TDEE calculator is accurate — they are all estimates based on population formulas. Accuracy depends on how the calculator handles activity level and whether it can be calibrated against real results. Calculeat and MacroFactor are the only free alternatives that adjust your TDEE based on actual weight changes — and are therefore more accurate over time than static calculators like TDEECalculator.net.

faq.question: Is TDEECalculator.net better than Calculeat?
faq.answer: TDEECalculator.net is a good tool for a quick one-off estimate. Calculeat is better if you're actually going to use the TDEE result — it connects directly to your calorie goal, adapts it per phase (cut/bulk/maintenance) and calibrates against your weight data. TDEECalculator.net gives you a number. Calculeat gives you an actionable goal.

faq.question: Why do different TDEE calculators give different results?
faq.answer: The differences come from three factors: which BMR formula is used (Mifflin-St Jeor, Harris-Benedict, Katch-McArdle), how activity levels are defined (some are more generous than others), and whether the calculator accounts for NEAT and training volume separately.

faq.question: How do you know if your TDEE is accurate?
faq.answer: Log calories exactly for 2–3 weeks and measure your weight change daily (morning, fasting). If you eat 2200 kcal and your weight is stable, your TDEE is approximately 2200. If you lose 0.3 kg/week, your actual TDEE is approximately 2200 + 330 = 2530 kcal. This method — called metabolic calibration — is more accurate than any formula and is built into Calculeat.

faq.question: How often should you update your calorie needs?
faq.answer: Every 4–6 weeks if you're actively trying to change your body. TDEE changes with body weight, muscle mass, training volume and adaptive thermogenesis. A static calculator you used at the start won't be accurate after 12 weeks of cutting. Calculeat continuously updates your calorie goal based on actual weight trends — you don't need to recalculate manually.
